claims.text: An equiatomic CoCrFeNi alloy can exist as a single-phase FCC solid solution.
The initial alloy has equiaxed grains and no secondary phases in a solution-annealed or as-cast condition.
Room-temperature tensile plasticity is primarily governed by edge and mixed-character dislocation glide on FCC {111} planes.
The quaternary alloy has a moderate stacking-fault energy.
Moderate stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation twinning while permitting substantial strain hardening.
Below 0.3 Tm, yield strength has only weak strain-rate dependence because FCC dislocation glide is predominantly athermal.
Between strain rates of 10^-4 and 10^-1 s^-1, yield strength remains within 5% of its value at 10^-3 s^-1.
Stacking-fault energy controls the separation width of partial dislocations.
Stacking-fault energy controls the competition among slip, cross-slip, and deformation twinning.
The low Peierls barrier for edge dislocations in FCC alloys causes low-temperature strain-rate insensitivity.
In BCC alloys, thermally activated screw-dislocation mobility is rate-limiting.
CoCrFeMnNi and CoCrFeNi evidence shows dominant dislocation slip in the absence of twinning or phase transformation.
Dislocation forest hardening produces moderate-to-high strain hardening.
No significant FCC-to-HCP transformation occurs during tensile deformation under the stated conditions.
Exceptionally low stacking-fault energy can cause deformation twinning at higher strains.
Above 0.3 Tm, thermally activated cross-slip becomes significant and the proposed rate-insensitive boundary may fail.
Minor compositional fluctuations can change stacking-fault energy and shift the transition between slip-dominated and twinning-dominated deformation.
A yield-strength increase greater than 10% with increasing strain rate indicates thermally activated screw-dislocation motion typical of BCC behavior.
Direct observation of dominant FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC transformation rather than dislocation glide would falsify the proposed glide mechanism.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires yield strength to remain within 5% of the reference value, but falsification requires an increase greater than 10%, leaving changes between 5% and 10% unclassified.
